name: Rumtek
tagline: The Karmapa's seat in exile, across the valley from Gangtok
meta_description: Rumtek Monastery near Gangtok: its 1966 rebuilding by the 16th Karmapa, the golden stupa, Lingdum nearby, how to get there and what a half day costs.
summary: Rumtek is a village and monastery at about 1,500 m, 24 km from Gangtok across the Ranipool valley. Its Dharma Chakra Centre, rebuilt by the 16th Karmapa and inaugurated in 1966, is the largest monastery in Sikkim. Most people come for a half day by taxi for ₹1,500–2,500; a night here is quieter than Gangtok.

local_story.title: A ruined gompa and a Karmapa in exile
paras: The first monastery at Rumtek was built in the mid-18th century under the direction of Changchub Dorje, the 12th Karmapa, head of the Karma Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism. For a time it served as the main seat of that lineage in Sikkim. By the 20th century it had fallen into ruin. Then, in 1959, as thousands fled Tibet, Rangjung Rigpe Dorje, the 16th Karmapa, crossed into Sikkim with monks, relics and sacred objects from Tsurphu, his monastery near Lhasa.

He was offered other sites but chose the old ruin at Rumtek. The account kept by the monastery says he saw in it the right signs: streams flowing, hills behind, snow peaks in front and a river below. With help from the Sikkim royal family and local people, building took about four years. On Losar, the Tibetan New Year, in 1966, the Karmapa inaugurated the new seat, the Dharma Chakra Centre, and installed the relics brought from Tsurphu. He died in 1981, and a golden stupa at Rumtek holds his relics.

Since the 1990s Rumtek has been at the centre of the dispute over who is the true 17th Karmapa, a dispute that reached the Indian courts. Neither of the two rival candidates lives at Rumtek. The visible result for visitors is the armed security at the gate, where you show a photo ID. Inside, life goes on as it has since 1966: young monks at their lessons, prayers in the main hall, and the Karma Shri Nalanda Institute across the courtyard.

did_you_know: Rumtek's new monastery was inaugurated by the 16th Karmapa on Losar, the Tibetan New Year, in 1966, after about four years of building.
The first Rumtek monastery dates from the mid-18th century and was built under Changchub Dorje, the 12th Karmapa; it lay in ruins by 1959.
Lingdum, also called Ranka or Pal Zurmang Kagyud Monastery, a short drive from Rumtek, was completed in 1999 and follows the Zurmang Kagyu tradition.
intro: Rumtek sits on the far side of the valley from Gangtok, so close that you can see its roofs from the Gangtok ridge on a clear day, yet nearly an hour away by road. The drive drops to Ranipool and climbs again through farms and forest. The monastery stands at the top of a village of small shops and houses, with a long walk-up from the gate. It is the largest monastery in Sikkim and still a working seat of the Karma Kagyu school, so expect monks at prayer and lessons rather than a museum.

Most visitors give Rumtek two or three hours on a half-day taxi trip from Gangtok, often adding Lingdum Monastery at Ranka on the way back. That is enough to see the main hall, the golden stupa and the courtyard. We think it is worth slowing down: come for the morning or afternoon prayers, walk down to the old monastery below, or spend a night in the village, where evenings are quiet and the lights of Gangtok shine across the valley.
facts: Karma Kagyu seat, golden stupa, monk college
costs: Half-day reserved taxi from Gangtok, Rumtek and Lingdum
Shared taxi seat from Gangtok, where available
Free or a small fee · photo ID needed
Tea and momos in the village

highlights.title: The main prayer hall
highlights.text: The Dharma Chakra Centre's main hall is built in the style of Tsurphu, the Karmapa's monastery in Tibet, with painted pillars, thangkas and a large seated Buddha. Visitors may watch prayers from the side if they keep quiet. Photography inside is often not allowed, so ask first and follow the signs.

highlights.title: The golden stupa
highlights.text: Behind the main hall, a small building holds the golden stupa that contains the relics of the 16th Karmapa, who rebuilt Rumtek and died in 1981. Monks guard it, and a donation is customary. Walk round it clockwise, and leave shoes and hats outside.

highlights.title: The monk college
highlights.text: Opposite the stupa is the Karma Shri Nalanda Institute for Higher Buddhist Studies, where monks study philosophy, debate and ritual over several years. You see young monks crossing the courtyard with books and robes flying. It is a working college, so do not wander into classrooms.

highlights.title: Old Rumtek below the village
highlights.text: A short way below the new monastery stands the older Rumtek gompa, on the site of the 18th-century foundation. It is smaller, quieter and less visited, and the walk down through the village takes about 20–30 minutes. Ask a shopkeeper for the path.

highlights.title: Lingdum on the way back
highlights.text: Lingdum, or Ranka Monastery, was completed in 1999 and follows the Zurmang Kagyu tradition. Its wide courtyard and painted halls are often busier with young monks than visitors. Taxis link it with Rumtek in a single half-day trip from Gangtok.

highlights.title: A night across the valley
highlights.text: Rumtek is a good place to sleep if Gangtok's traffic wears you out. After the day visitors leave, the village goes quiet, prayer flags snap in the evening wind, and the lights of Gangtok come up across the valley. Mornings bring monks' horns from the monastery.

how_to_reach.text: The easy way is a half-day reserved taxi from Gangtok, about ₹1,500–2,500 depending on season and whether you add Lingdum. The drive is about 24 km and an hour each way via Ranipool. Agree the stops and waiting time before you leave.

Some shared taxis run between Gangtok and Rumtek village, mostly in the morning and early afternoon, for about ₹60–120 a seat. They are irregular and fill slowly, so ask your hotel where they leave from that season and do not rely on a late return.

Rumtek is reached by turning off NH10 at Ranipool, a few kilometres below Gangtok. If you are coming up from Siliguri in a reserved car, you can stop at Rumtek on the way, adding about two hours, though most drivers prefer to reach Gangtok first.

where_to_stay: Most travellers visit Rumtek from Gangtok and do not stay. For a night, there are a few simple guesthouses and homestays in Rumtek village near the monastery gate, run by local families, with plain rooms and home food; ask in the village or through your Gangtok hotel, as few are listed online. For more comfort, Bamboo Retreat sits on the slope below Rumtek among farms and forest, with organic food and quiet rooms, at Comfort prices. Gangtok is an hour away, with every budget from dorms to family hotels.
tips: Carry a photo ID for the security check at the monastery gate.
Dress modestly, remove shoes and hats before entering halls, and walk clockwise round stupas and prayer wheels.
Ask before taking photographs inside the halls; many areas do not allow cameras.
Come in the morning for prayers and clearer views back towards Gangtok.
Combine Rumtek with Lingdum in one half-day taxi to save a second trip.

experiences.title: Morning prayers in Rumtek's main hall
experiences.summary: Sit at the side of the main hall at Rumtek while the monks chant the morning prayers, with drums, cymbals and long horns. It is the best way to see the monastery as a working seat of the Karma Kagyu school rather than a sight.
body: Rumtek's day begins early. In the main hall of the Dharma Chakra Centre the monks gather in rows facing one another, wrapped in maroon robes, and chant prayers to a rhythm of drums and cymbals, broken now and then by the deep sound of long horns. Young monks bring butter tea down the rows. Prayer times vary with the season and the monastery calendar, so ask at the gate or your hotel the day before.

Visitors are allowed to sit quietly near the entrance or at the side. Take off your shoes and hat, keep your phone silent, and do not walk between the monks or in front of the altar. Photography during prayers is usually not allowed. If you are unsure, watch what the Tibetan and Sikkimese visitors do and follow them. A small donation or a butter lamp offering is welcome but not expected.

To be at Rumtek for the morning session you need either a night in the village or an early taxi from Gangtok, leaving around 6 am. In return you get the monastery before the day visitors arrive, clear light on the hills and the view across to Gangtok. Afterwards, walk the courtyard, see the golden stupa when it opens, and have tea in one of the small shops by the gate.

faqs.q: What time are the prayers at Rumtek?
faqs.a: Prayer times at Rumtek change with the season and the monastery calendar, but there is usually an early-morning session and another in the afternoon. Ask at the monastery gate, your hotel or the village shops the day before. If you visit only in the middle of the day, the hall may be quiet.

faqs.q: Can visitors sit inside during prayers?
faqs.a: Usually yes, near the entrance or at the side of the hall, if you are quiet and respectful. Remove shoes and hats, keep phones silent and do not walk in front of the monks or the altar. Photography during prayers is generally not allowed. Follow any instruction from the monks.

faqs.q: Is there a dress code at Rumtek?
faqs.a: There is no formal code, but dress modestly: cover shoulders and knees, and avoid short skirts and vests. Remove shoes and hats before entering halls. Carry a photo ID for the security check at the gate. Walk clockwise round stupas and prayer wheels, as the Sikkimese do.

experiences.title: The golden stupa and the monks' college
experiences.cost: Free · donation customary at the stupa
experiences.summary: Behind Rumtek's main hall a small shrine holds the golden stupa with the relics of the 16th Karmapa, who rebuilt the monastery. Across the courtyard is the Karma Shri Nalanda Institute, where monks train for years in Buddhist philosophy.
body: The 16th Karmapa, Rangjung Rigpe Dorje, died in 1981, fifteen years after he inaugurated the new Rumtek. His relics rest in a golden stupa inside a small building behind the main hall. It is the most revered object at Rumtek, and monks watch over it. When the shrine is open you may enter quietly, walk round the stupa clockwise and offer a khata, the white scarf, or a small donation. Opening hours vary, so do not be surprised if it is closed for a ritual.

Facing it is the Karma Shri Nalanda Institute for Higher Buddhist Studies, a college where monks study philosophy, logic, debate and ritual over many years. You may see students debating in pairs in the courtyard, clapping their hands to make a point, or crossing with stacks of loose-leaf texts. It is a working college and not open for tours, but the courtyard gives you a sense of the place.

Between the two, take time to look at the building itself: the painted eaves, the gold roof ornaments and the prayer wheels along the walls. The design follows Tsurphu, the Karmapa's seat in Tibet, which is one reason the monastery feels so large for a hillside village. Keep to the paths, keep your voice down and ask before photographing any monk.

faqs.q: Whose relics are in the golden stupa at Rumtek?
faqs.a: The golden stupa at Rumtek holds the relics of Rangjung Rigpe Dorje, the 16th Karmapa, who rebuilt the monastery after leaving Tibet in 1959 and inaugurated it in 1966. He died in 1981. Visitors may enter quietly when the shrine is open, walk round clockwise and offer a scarf or small donation.

faqs.q: Can we visit the monk college at Rumtek?
faqs.a: The Karma Shri Nalanda Institute is a working college for monks, not a museum, so classrooms are not open to visitors. You can see it from the courtyard and often watch students crossing or debating outside. Keep a respectful distance and ask before photographing anyone.

faqs.q: Is photography allowed at Rumtek?
faqs.a: Photography is usually allowed in the courtyard and outside the buildings, but often not inside the main hall or the stupa shrine. Signs and monks will tell you. Ask before photographing any monk, and never use a flash during prayers. Drones are not allowed.

experiences.title: Down to old Rumtek through the village
experiences.summary: A short walk downhill from the new monastery through Rumtek village to the older gompa on the site of the 18th-century foundation. It is quieter than the main monastery and shows the village behind the sight: kitchen gardens, prayer flags and small shrines.
body: Before 1959 Rumtek had only the old monastery, built in the mid-18th century under the 12th Karmapa and later left in poor repair. The 16th Karmapa built his new seat higher up, but the old site was kept and restored, and a smaller gompa stands there today. Few day visitors go down, which is exactly why we like it: you are more likely to meet a caretaker monk or a village woman turning the prayer wheels than a tour group.

The walk starts outside the gate of the new monastery and drops through the village on a mix of road and path, past houses with cardamom and vegetable plots, chortens and strings of prayer flags. Allow 20–30 minutes down and a little longer back up. Ask a shopkeeper for the way, because the path is not signposted. The gompa may be locked; if so, walk round it clockwise and enjoy the quiet.

Go in the morning, when the light is good and the village is busy with school children and farm work, or in the late afternoon, when it softens. Wear shoes with grip, as some steps are steep and slippery after rain. On the way back up, the tea shops near the gate make a good stop for momos and a cup of tea before your taxi.

faqs.q: Is the old Rumtek monastery worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you have an extra hour. The old monastery is smaller and simpler than the main Rumtek seat, but it is quiet, rarely crowded and stands on the site of the 18th-century foundation. The walk through the village is half the pleasure. It may be locked at times.

faqs.q: How far is old Rumtek from the new monastery?
faqs.a: It is a short walk below the new monastery, about 20–30 minutes downhill through the village and a little longer back up. The path is not signposted, so ask a shopkeeper near the gate. A taxi can also drop you, but the walk is the point.

faqs.q: Is the village walk suitable for older travellers?
faqs.a: It is manageable for most fit older travellers who go slowly, but the return is uphill and some steps are steep and slippery in wet weather. Wear shoes with grip and carry water. Anyone who finds hills hard can ask their taxi to collect them below.

experiences.title: Lingdum Monastery on the Ranka road
experiences.summary: Lingdum, also called Ranka or Pal Zurmang Kagyud Monastery, was completed in 1999 and sits about an hour's drive from Gangtok. Most taxis combine it with Rumtek in a half day. Its wide courtyard and painted halls are often full of young monks.
body: Lingdum is a young monastery by Sikkim's standards. It was completed in 1999 and follows the Zurmang Kagyu tradition, a branch of the Kagyu school whose home monastery is in eastern Tibet. It stands on a forested slope near Ranka, about an hour's drive from Gangtok, and most taxis bring visitors here on the way to or from Rumtek, since the two roads meet below.

What sets Lingdum apart is its space. A broad paved courtyard opens in front of the main hall, which is richly painted inside with murals and a large Buddha. Young monks study and play here, and in the afternoon you may hear the evening prayers begin. The setting is green and quiet, and on clear days the hills fall away towards the Ranipool valley.

Visiting follows the same rules as Rumtek: shoes and hats off before entering, quiet voices, clockwise circuits and no photography where the signs say so. A donation is welcome. Ask your taxi driver to wait at least an hour. Come in the afternoon if you can, when the light is soft and the monks gather for prayers, and the courtyard is calm after the morning visitors leave.

faqs.q: How far is Lingdum Monastery from Gangtok?
faqs.a: Lingdum is about an hour's drive from Gangtok near Ranka. Most visitors take a half-day reserved taxi that covers both Lingdum and Rumtek for about ₹1,500–2,500, depending on season. Shared taxis to Ranka exist but are irregular, so a reserved car is far simpler.

faqs.q: When was Lingdum Monastery built?
faqs.a: Lingdum, also known as Ranka Monastery or Pal Zurmang Kagyud Monastery, was completed in 1999. It follows the Zurmang Kagyu tradition. Compared with Rumtek, it is younger, quieter and has a wider courtyard, and young monks are often studying or playing there in the afternoon.

faqs.q: Can we see Rumtek and Lingdum in one trip?
faqs.a: Yes. They are close to each other and most Gangtok taxis combine them in a half day of about four to five hours, including the drive and time at each. Start with Rumtek in the morning and stop at Lingdum on the way back for the afternoon prayers.

faqs.q: How far is Rumtek Monastery from Gangtok?
faqs.a: Rumtek is about 24 km from Gangtok, roughly an hour each way by road via Ranipool, even though it looks close across the valley. A half-day reserved taxi costs about ₹1,500–2,500 and can include Lingdum Monastery. Shared taxis exist but are irregular and slow to fill.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Rumtek?
faqs.a: Entry to Rumtek has been free or a small fee in recent years, but you must show a photo ID at the security check at the gate. Donations at the golden stupa and butter lamp offerings are at your choice. Fees and rules change, so carry a little cash and an ID.

faqs.q: Why is there security at Rumtek?
faqs.a: Rumtek has been at the centre of the dispute over the 17th Karmapa since the 1990s, with rival groups claiming the monastery, and there were clashes in the past. Indian security forces guard the gate and check IDs. It does not affect visitors beyond the short check, so keep your ID handy.

faqs.q: How much time do we need at Rumtek?
faqs.a: Two to three hours at the monastery is enough for the main hall, the golden stupa and the courtyard, plus an hour for Lingdum on the way back. A half day from Gangtok covers both. Add a night in the village if you want to see morning prayers without an early taxi.

faqs.q: Can we stay overnight at Rumtek?
faqs.a: Yes. Rumtek village has a few simple guesthouses and homestays near the monastery gate, and Bamboo Retreat on the slope below offers Comfort-level rooms with meals. A night here is quiet, and you can join early prayers. Most budget travellers still stay in Gangtok, an hour away.

faqs.q: Is Rumtek worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, especially if you are interested in Tibetan Buddhism. Rumtek is the largest monastery in Sikkim and the seat in exile of the Karmapa, rebuilt by the 16th Karmapa and inaugurated in 1966. Come for prayers rather than a quick photo, and add Lingdum on the same trip.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Rumtek?
faqs.a: October to December and March to May give the clearest days and the best views back to Gangtok. Losar, the Tibetan New Year in February or March, brings protector dances before the festival. The monastery is open all year, but monsoon rain from June to September makes the road slow.

faqs.q: Is Rumtek suitable for children and older people?
faqs.a: Yes. The monastery is at about 1,500 m, lower than Gangtok, and the main sights are close together. There is an uphill walk from the gate to the main hall that takes 10–15 minutes, which older travellers can take slowly. Children should be told to keep quiet in the halls.

faqs.q: Which festivals are held at Rumtek?
faqs.a: Rumtek celebrates Losar, the Tibetan New Year, in February or March, with protector dances in the days before it, and other ritual dances through the year on dates set by the Tibetan lunar calendar. Ask the monastery or a Gangtok operator for the year's dates, and check current status before you travel.
